clue.text: Obscure diarist

parts.note: Charles Pooter keeps the diary in the Grossmiths' comic novel, a humdrum clerk who calls himself a person of no account in its title

explanation.surface: A request to name some little-known keeper of a journal.
explanation.walkthrough: The Diary of a Nobody (1892) by George and Weedon Grossmith is the diary of the suburban clerk Charles Pooter, as obscure a diarist as could be.
explanation.definitionFit: The book's title gives its humble diarist the label of a person of no importance, which is what an obscure man is.

clue.text: Lotuses provided for what may be noble sum

indicators.note: the clue says the answer is what these words may become once their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Lotus flowers bought for whatever a grand amount of money might be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'what may be' tells you that the lotus word is what NOBLE SUM could turn into when its letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Nelumbo is the botanical genus of the sacred lotus, so its plural names the plants.

clue.text: Large sort of legs for flying ace

parts.note: large means big

indicators.note: a sort of legs is the word's letters sorted into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone with big, oddly shaped legs is praised as a fighter pilot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Large' looks like part of a description of legs; 'sort of' is the signal to rearrange. Biggles is the hero of W. E. Johns's boys' books.
explanation.definitionFit: Biggles is Captain James Bigglesworth, W. E. Johns's fictional fighter pilot hero of countless boys' books.

clue.text: Your old place in terribly dim bar suggests rapturous poem

indicators.note: in places the archaic pronoun inside the rearranged letters of the other words
terribly suggests the words dim bar are messed up and reordered

parts.note: thy is the old form of your

explanation.surface: Somebody's former home in a gloomy pub inspires an ecstatic verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Your old' is the archaic second-person form, and 'terribly' rearranges 'dim bar' around it; 'in' marks the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: A dithyramb was originally a wild Greek choral hymn to Dionysus, hence any ecstatic, impassioned poem.

clue.text: Folk like Leibniz and Pangloss?

parts.note: Leibniz held this to be the best of all possible worlds and Voltaire's Pangloss in Candide parrots him; both imagine an ideal state of things

explanation.surface: A question about what kind of people a philosopher and a fictional tutor were.
explanation.walkthrough: Pangloss, the tutor in Voltaire's Candide, satirises Leibniz's optimism; the question mark admits that idealists of this stamp are visionaries of a perfect world rather than literal planners.
explanation.definitionFit: Believers in a perfect society are visionary idealists, and Leibniz's best possible world is that dream stated as philosophy.

clue.text: 9's ragamuffin

explanation.surface: A Nobel novelist's scruffy urchin.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 is the answer to 9 down, the novelist; his collection of stories published in 1920 bears this title.
explanation.definitionFit: Galsworthy's 1920 story collection has this title, and the word itself means a person in ragged clothes, a scruffy urchin.

clue.text: Outstanding, like Fred Urquhart's captive lady

explanation.surface: A remarkable heroine imprisoned in a Scottish novelist's book.
explanation.walkthrough: Fred Urquhart, a Scottish writer, published the novel Proud Lady in a Cage (1980); 'captive lady' points to the caged heroine of that title.
explanation.definitionFit: Something standing out from a surface is said to project, and Urquhart's caged heroine carries the same adjective in his title.

clue.text: Symphonic poet with Bohemian lifestyle

parts.note: a writer of symphonic poems who was literally a Bohemian, born in the Czech lands, author of Ma vlast and the quartet From My Life

explanation.surface: A poet who writes in symphonies and lives like an unconventional artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bohemian' suggests an artistic, carefree way of living, but it means from Bohemia; 'poet' is a composer of symphonic poems, and 'lifestyle' recalls his quartet From My Life.
explanation.definitionFit: The Czech composer Bedrich Smetana wrote the cycle of symphonic poems Ma vlast and was born in Bohemia.

clue.text: French painter portrays young relative with ancient line

parts.note: sis is short for sister, a young relative
a ley is a supposed straight line linking ancient sites

explanation.surface: An artist from France paints a younger family member beside an old track.
explanation.walkthrough: A ley line is an alignment of prehistoric sites, often claimed to hold mystical power.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Sisley was an Impressionist landscape painter, born in Paris to English parents.

clue.text: Nobel Prizewinner said to have shown foresight

definitions.text: Nobel Prizewinner said to have shown foresight

parts.words: Nobel Prizewinner said to have shown foresight
parts.note: foresight sounds like the surname of the family in the novelist's famous saga, so the Nobel laureate is one who put that family on show

explanation.surface: A Nobel laureate who supposedly saw the future coming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foresight' is said like Forsyte: the 1932 Nobel laureate wrote The Forsyte Saga, so he 'showed Forsytes'.
explanation.definitionFit: The English novelist and playwright won the 1932 Nobel Prize in Literature, chiefly for The Forsyte Saga.

clue.text: Nance, Patrick White's golden-hearted girl, inverts stage illumination

indicators.note: inverts here means the two halves of the word swap places, its front moving to the back

parts.note: a footlight is one of the lamps along the front of a stage

explanation.surface: A kind-hearted woman in an Australian novel flips the lights of a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inverts' does not reverse the letters: it swaps the two halves of the stage word, its front half moving behind the back. Nance Lightfoot is the warm-hearted prostitute in Patrick White's fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Patrick White gives his kind, golden-hearted character Nance this surname, so the girl is named by it.

clue.text: Playwright's name recalled during wasted opening night .

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the letters found are read in the opposite direction
during says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A dramatist's name is remembered while a premiere goes badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'during' finds STEDO inside 'waSTED Opening', and 'recalled' turns it round. Clifford Odets was an American playwright (Waiting for Lefty).
explanation.definitionFit: Clifford Odets was the American dramatist of Waiting for Lefty and Golden Boy, so the surname is a playwright's.

clue.text: Burgess trilogy from Curious Animal, a Yankee and Other Stories

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows, unbroken

parts.words: Curious Animal, a Yankee and Other Stories

explanation.surface: A Burgess trilogy apparently drawn from an oddly titled story collection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' points inside the invented book title: 'animAL A YANkee' holds the answer, spanning three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Burgess's three early novels set in colonial Malaya were collected as The Malayan Trilogy.

clue.text: Beckett work possibly leading to a mate

explanation.surface: A Beckett play that might end in checkmate.
explanation.walkthrough: In chess the final phase of the game, with few pieces left, may finish with one king mated.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Beckett's one-act play of 1957 has this title, and the closing stage of a chess match can end in checkmate.

clue.text: Nameless bard, or Italian

indicators.note: nameless means without a name, so N, the usual abbreviation for name, is removed

parts.note: Ossian is the legendary Gaelic bard of Macpherson's poems

explanation.surface: An anonymous poet, or perhaps an Italian one.
explanation.walkthrough: Ossian is the legendary Gaelic bard of James Macpherson's 1760s 'translations'; 'Nameless' drops N, the standard abbreviation for name. The definition reads 'Italian for or'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ossia is the Italian word meaning 'or else', used in music for an alternative passage.

clue.text: Adam Hornbrook's " civic dignitary, Ralph

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, "Adam Hornbrook's \" civic dignitary, Ralph (8)", has lost the words after the quotation mark (likely a title from Thomas Cooper's Adam Hornbook); no scan, and searching found nothing to restore it.

clue.text: Successful college boat described by Robert Hillyer?

definitions.text: Successful college boat described by Robert Hillyer?

parts.words: Successful college boat described by Robert Hillyer?
parts.note: in college rowing the leading boat finishes Head of the River, and Robert Hillyer, an American poet, wrote a 1932 novel with a title made of those two words

explanation.surface: A winning college rowing crew, as portrayed by an American poet.
explanation.walkthrough: In British college rowing the crew that ends the bumps races on top is 'Head of the River'; Hillyer's novel title puts the same two words the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Hillyer's 1932 novel bears this title, and the top crew in a bumps race goes Head of the River.

clue.text: Successful takeover bidders, like Antonio of Milan, and Duke Frederick

definitions.text: Successful takeover bidders, like Antonio of Milan, and Duke Frederick

parts.words: Successful takeover bidders, like Antonio of Milan, and Duke Frederick
parts.note: Antonio seizes his brother Prospero's dukedom in The Tempest, and Duke Frederick drives out his brother in As You Like It; both grab power wrongfully

explanation.surface: Winning corporate raiders are compared to two Shakespearean schemers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takeover bidders' sounds like the stock market, but means men who seize thrones: Shakespeare's Antonio and Duke Frederick each oust a brother.
explanation.definitionFit: People who seize a throne or power without right are usurpers, as Antonio and Frederick both did.

clue.text: "Home went Violante and ed all " (Browning)

parts.note: a line from Browning's The Ring and the Book with a word left out before the letters ed: Violante went home and poured out all her secrets

explanation.surface: A quotation from Browning with a gap for the solver to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap stands before 'ed': the answer plus -ed fills it, Violante confessing everything to her husband in The Ring and the Book.
explanation.definitionFit: To open the heart and confess freely is the sense needed to complete Browning's line about Violante telling everything.

clue.text: Sort of research carried out by Jules Verne?

definitions.text: Sort of research carried out by Jules Verne?

parts.words: Sort of research carried out by Jules Verne?
parts.note: thorough research is described with this phrase, and Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea went literally deep below the waves

explanation.surface: Asking what kind of investigation a French novelist undertook.
explanation.walkthrough: Thorough study is called 'in-depth'; Verne's Captain Nemo explores literally at depth in Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Detailed, thorough research is called this, and Verne's submarine voyage took place far below the ocean surface.

clue.text: A man writing a panegyric may keep them out of sight, suggested Samuel Johnson

definitions.text: A man writing a panegyric may keep them out of sight, suggested Samuel Johnson

parts.words: A man writing a panegyric may keep them out of sight, suggested Samuel Johnson
parts.note: Johnson remarked that a writer of praise may conceal a subject's failings; the hidden things are the faults of character

explanation.surface: Dr Johnson's advice on what a eulogist should leave unmentioned.
explanation.walkthrough: Johnson observed that 'a man who writes a panegyric may keep vices out of sight', unlike a biographer who must tell all.
explanation.definitionFit: Moral failings or bad habits are the faults a eulogist would leave unmentioned.

clue.text: Star port of ancient Egypt

explanation.surface: A celebrated harbour of the Pharaohs.
explanation.walkthrough: One name serves both a bright star in the constellation Carina and a coastal town near Alexandria.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the second brightest star in the night sky and also an ancient Egyptian harbour town at the Nile's western mouth.

clue.text: "I should ("be proud to have my memory anna Akhmatova", Epilogue)

definitions.text: "I should ("be proud to have my memory anna Akhmatova", Epilogue)

parts.words: "I should ("be proud to have my memory anna Akhmatova", Epilogue)
parts.note: a line from the Epilogue to Anna Akhmatova's Requiem with a word missing after memory, the poet saying she would be honoured to be remembered

explanation.surface: A quotation from Akhmatova with a word left for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed text has run the missing word into 'Anna'; the gap after 'memory' is filled by the answer, the poet imagining a monument honouring her.
explanation.definitionFit: To honour or adorn something is the sense that completes the line about Akhmatova's memory being dignified.

clue.text: Random father

parts.note: the hero of Smollett's Roderick Random finally finds his long-lost father, who has made a fortune in South America under a Spanish name

explanation.surface: A father picked at random.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Random' is not an adjective but Roderick Random, Smollett's 1748 hero, whose father reappears as the rich Don of the Spanish form of Roderick.
explanation.definitionFit: Roderick Random's father is known in the novel by the Spanish form of his son's first name.

clue.text: Passage from it inconclusive for Mrs Moore

definitions.text: Passage from it inconclusive for Mrs Moore

parts.words: Passage from it inconclusive for Mrs Moore
parts.note: Mrs Moore makes her passage to this country in Forster's novel, but she dies on the voyage away from it, and the Marabar caves episode is never resolved

explanation.surface: A journey whose meaning remains unsettled for an elderly lady.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Moore is the elderly visitor in E. M. Forster's A Passage to India; her passage out of the country ends with her death at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Forster's novel takes Mrs Moore on a passage to this subcontinent, the country named in its title.

clue.text: Give short-story writer a ring. If you can remember his name

definitions.text: Give short-story writer a ring. If you can remember his name

parts.words: Give short-story writer a ring. If you can remember his name
parts.note: the American humorist and short-story writer's first name was Ring, so giving him a ring supplies his forename

explanation.surface: Telephone a story writer, provided you can recall what he is called.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give a ring' seems to mean phone, but Ring was the American writer's first name: Ring Lardner, author of You Know Me Al.
explanation.definitionFit: Ring Lardner was an American sportswriter and celebrated short-story writer.

clue.text: Unconscious follow-up to trophy for heart doctor

indicators.note: follow-up to puts the unconscious part after the trophy word

parts.note: a cup is a trophy
in Freud the id is the unconscious part of the mind

explanation.surface: After winning a cup, a cardiologist goes into a faint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heart doctor' suggests a cardiologist; it is the god of love, who deals in affairs of the heart.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman god of love treats lovers' hearts with his arrows, so he is a doctor of the heart.

clue.text: A couple of Milne's works

explanation.surface: A pair of books by the creator of Winnie-the-Pooh.
explanation.walkthrough: A. A. Milne wrote a 1931 novel with this title, besides the Pooh books.
explanation.definitionFit: A pair of persons is a couple, and Milne's 1931 novel about a married pair is titled with the same phrase.

clue.text: No Haydn I played recalled Hungarian pianist

indicators.note: played suggests the letters of the words are performed in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A Hungarian pianist recalled refusing to perform Haydn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'played' rearranges NO HAYDN I. Erno Dohnanyi was a Hungarian pianist, composer and conductor.
explanation.definitionFit: Erno Dohnanyi was a celebrated Hungarian concert pianist as well as a composer.

clue.text: Overdose of good degrees for somewhat long-winded poets

parts.note: good degrees are firsts, written 1sts, with the figure 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: Too much of top university honours suits wordy poets.
explanation.walkthrough: Top degrees are firsts, written 1STS; read the 1 as an I to get ISTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers of odes, lofty and often lengthy lyrical poems, are the poets meant.
